Ancient Egypt
column3: Pharaohs, pyramids and the gift of the Nile.

column2: Built about 4,500 years ago, it was the tallest building on Earth for some 3,800 years.
The pharaoh who built the Great Pyramid; the only complete statue of him ever found is just 7.5 centimetres tall.
He ruled for 66 years and put up giant statues of himself all over Egypt.
One of the few women to rule Egypt as pharaoh; some statues show her with a king's false beard.
A pharaoh who tried to make Egyptians worship a single sun god, the Aten.
Egypt's last queen spoke many languages and was the first of her family to learn Egyptian.
Africa's longest river: its yearly flood left rich black mud for farming.
The same message in three scripts helped scholars finally read hieroglyphs in 1822.
Two temples carved into a cliff, cut into blocks and moved uphill in the 1960s to save them from a new lake.
The terraced temple of Queen Hatshepsut, built against the cliffs near Luxor.
An Egyptian maths book about 3,600 years old, full of puzzles about bread, beer and pyramids.
Ancient Greece
column3: Thinkers, athletes and the first democracy.

column2: A marble temple for the goddess Athena, built on a hill above Athens nearly 2,500 years ago.
The city where citizens first voted on their own laws, in a democracy.
A king of Sparta who led his 300 Spartans at the pass of Thermopylae in 480 BCE.
The poet said to have told the stories of the Trojan War and of Odysseus' long voyage home.
He taught by asking questions, and he never wrote a single book.
A pupil of Socrates who started one of the first schools, the Academy.
He studied everything from animals and plants to poetry, and he taught Alexander the Great.
By the age of 30 he ruled an empire that stretched from Greece to India.
Held at Olympia every four years for more than a thousand years, with races, wrestling and chariots.
A bronze statue of the sun god about as tall as a ten-storey building; an earthquake toppled it.
One of the Seven Wonders, its fire guided ships into harbour for many centuries.
Ancient Rome
column3: Emperors, legions and roads that led everywhere.

column2: A famous general who became master of Rome; the month of July is named after him.
Rome's greatest speaker; hundreds of his letters still survive.
Rome's great enemy, who marched an army with elephants across the Alps.
The busy heart of the city, full of temples, law courts and shops.
A stone road begun in 312 BCE; you can still walk along parts of it today.
Under this emperor the Roman Empire reached its largest size.
An emperor who wrote his thoughts in a notebook we still read, the Meditations.
An emperor who loved music and theatre, and even sang on stage himself.
A town buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, so well preserved that you can walk its streets.
The emperor who founded Constantinople, the city we now call Istanbul.
Knights and Castles
column3: Kings, queens and castles of the Middle Ages.

column2: He sailed from Normandy and won the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
A 70-metre-long embroidery that tells the story of 1066 like a comic strip.
She was queen of France and then queen of England, and the mother of two English kings.
Called the Lionheart, he spent only a few months of his reign in England.
An order of knights who were also monks, dressed in white with a red cross.
One of the best-preserved castles of the Crusades, high on a hill in Syria.
A farm girl from France who led an army when she was about 17.
A charter of 1215 which said that even the king had to obey the law.
Vikings
column3: Sailors, traders and explorers from the far north.

column2: A Viking explorer who reached North America about 500 years before Columbus.
He named his icy new home Greenland to make settlers want to go there.
The Norse god of thunder; Thursday is named after him.
A beautifully carved Viking ship found buried in a grave mound in Norway.
A Viking ship so well made that a copy sailed across the Atlantic in 1893.
The remains of a Viking settlement in Canada, about a thousand years old.
A stone carved with runes, the letters the Vikings wrote with.
An island monastery in England whose raid by Vikings in 793 shocked Europe.
Great Explorers
column3: Brave travellers who crossed oceans, deserts and mountains.

column2: A Chinese monk who walked all the way to India and back to collect books.
A merchant from Venice who travelled to China and wrote a famous book about it.
He travelled for nearly 30 years across Africa and Asia, further than anyone else of his time.
A Chinese admiral who led huge fleets across the Indian Ocean; his treasure ships are said to be among the largest wooden ships ever built.
A Portuguese prince who sent ships down the coast of Africa, though he rarely sailed himself.
In 1492 he sailed across the Atlantic, hoping to reach Asia.
The first European to sail all the way from Europe to India, in 1498.
His fleet was the first to sail around the whole world, though he died on the way.
A British captain who mapped the coasts of New Zealand and eastern Australia.
Inventions and Ideas
column3: Clever ideas that changed how people live.

column2: One of the oldest written law codes, carved on a tall black stone nearly 3,800 years ago.
An ancient library that tried to collect a copy of every book it could find.
A Greek inventor who is said to have shouted "Eureka!" in his bath.
His geometry book was used in schools for more than 2,000 years.
A Chinese court official remembered for improving paper-making around the year 105.
A scholar in Baghdad whose name gave us the word "algorithm".
A great library and meeting place for scholars in Baghdad.
His printing press with movable metal letters made books far cheaper.
A painter and inventor who filled notebooks with designs for flying machines.
In 1610 he looked through his telescope and discovered four moons of Jupiter.
He explained gravity, the force that makes apples fall and keeps the Moon in orbit.
Amazing Buildings
column3: Wonders of stone, brick and marble from around the world.

column2: Built and rebuilt over 2,000 years, its walls run for thousands of kilometres.
A white marble tomb built by the emperor Shah Jahan for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
A vast temple in Cambodia, often called the largest religious monument in the world.
A giant Buddhist monument on the island of Java with more than 500 Buddha statues.
For nearly a thousand years it was the largest church in the world.
A palace in Granada famous for its gardens, fountains and patterned walls.
An Inca city high in the Andes mountains, built around 1450.
A city carved into pink sandstone cliffs in Jordan.
One of the largest pyramids in the world, in the ancient city of Teotihuacan in Mexico.
A stepped temple tower built about 4,000 years ago in what is now Iraq.
A red sandstone tower in Delhi about 73 metres tall, begun around the year 1200.
One of the Seven Wonders; no one has ever found it, and some think it was only a legend.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
The Great Pyramid was built from more than two million blocks of stone.
The Great Wall of China cannot really be seen from the Moon with your own eyes.
Vikings did not wear horned helmets in battle: that idea comes from costumes and paintings of the 1800s.
The first Olympic Games, according to Greek tradition, were held in 776 BCE.
Paper was invented in China about 2,000 years ago.
The Bayeux Tapestry is not really a tapestry at all: it is embroidered with wool on linen.
Napoleon was about 1.69 metres tall, ordinary for his time: the idea that he was very short is a myth.
At Pompeii, loaves of bread were found still in an oven, buried by the eruption of 79 CE.
Mansa Musa of Mali gave away so much gold on his way to Mecca in 1324 that its price fell in Cairo.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are the only one of the Seven Wonders whose site has never been found.
Roman concrete was so strong that buildings made with it are still standing nearly 2,000 years later.
Writing was invented in Mesopotamia more than 5,000 years ago, with marks pressed into wet clay.
William Shakespeare is the first known writer to use hundreds of English words.
Queen Elizabeth I could speak French, Italian and Latin, and she studied Greek too.
Leonardo da Vinci wrote many of his notes backwards, in mirror writing.
Tutankhamun became pharaoh when he was only about nine years old.
The Romans held a winter festival called Saturnalia, with feasts, games and presents.
The Maya kept two calendars at once, one of 260 days and one of 365 days.
Under Genghis Khan's sons and grandsons, the Mongol Empire became the largest land empire there has ever been.
Marco Polo amazed Europeans by describing paper money, which he had seen in China.
The Eiffel Tower was built for a world's fair in 1889 and was only meant to stand for 20 years.
Louis XIV of France reigned for 72 years, longer than any other European king.
Isaac Newton also ran England's Royal Mint and hunted down people who made fake coins.
Gutenberg printed his famous Bible in Mainz around 1455.
Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BCE with an army and about 37 elephants.
The Silk Road was not one road but a web of trade routes stretching across Asia.
Alexander the Great founded many cities called Alexandria; the most famous is in Egypt.
The Tower of London once kept a royal zoo, with lions and even a polar bear.
The ancient Egyptians loved cats, and many cats were mummified.
In Roman public toilets, people sat side by side on long stone benches.
China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, was buried with an army of thousands of life-size clay soldiers.
Actors in ancient Greek plays wore big masks so that everyone in the theatre could tell who they were playing.
The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, was built on an island in the middle of a lake.
Cyrus the Great of Persia is remembered for letting the peoples he conquered keep their own customs.
The Library of Alexandria may have held hundreds of thousands of scrolls.
Medieval castles had toilets called garderobes, which often emptied straight into the moat.
At the pyramid of Chichén Itzá in Mexico, the evening sun at the equinox makes a shadow like a snake.
Cleopatra came from a Greek family that ruled Egypt for nearly 300 years.
The Colosseum in Rome could hold at least 50,000 people.
Roman towns had snack bars that sold hot food to people in the street.
The oldest photograph that still survives was taken in France around 1826.
The Wright brothers' first powered flight, in 1903, lasted just 12 seconds.
The windows around the base of the Hagia Sophia's dome make it look as if it is floating.
The Inca had no alphabet, but they kept records with knotted strings called quipu.
Inca messengers ran in relays along mountain roads to carry news across the empire.
Queen Victoria was the first ruler of Britain to live in Buckingham Palace.
Peter the Great of Russia was more than two metres tall.
The ancient Egyptians made one of the first calendars with 365 days.
Kites were invented in China more than 2,000 years ago.
Chess began in India about 1,500 years ago, in a game called chaturanga.
The Rosetta Stone is a piece of a bigger stone: its top and one corner are missing.
Ancient Greek runners at Olympia raced in a stadium about 192 metres long.
The Statue of Liberty was a gift from the people of France to the United States in 1886.
Sparta's kings were always two at a time, from two different royal families.
The Vikings reached North America about a thousand years ago, at L'Anse aux Meadows in Canada.
Zheng He's fleet in 1405 had more than 200 ships and about 27,000 sailors and soldiers.
Ibn Battuta's travels covered about 120,000 kilometres, three times around the Earth.
The word "algorithm" comes from the name of the Baghdad scholar al-Khwarizmi.
In 1610 Galileo published drawings of the Moon's mountains and craters, seen through his own telescope.
Machu Picchu's finest walls were built without mortar: their stones are cut to fit together tightly.
The Taj Mahal took about 20 years and 20,000 workers to build.
